content: The text provided is a detailed and technical description of a systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the diagnostic accuracy of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for detecting hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies. 1. Background: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have achieved sustained virological response rates exceeding 90% in individuals treated for hepatitis C virus (HCV). However, a significant proportion of HCV-infected individuals remain undiagnosed and untreated. Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) have been widely used to detect HCV exposure, but their laboratory-based nature has posed challenges in reaching at-risk populations. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HCV antibody detection are commercially available and may facilitate decentralized HCV screening in non-laboratory settings. This review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of available assays for detecting HCV antibodies as biomarkers of exposure. 2. Methods: The review followed PRISMA guidelines and Cochrane recommendations. The search strategy was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42015023567). A comprehensive literature search was conducted across eight databases, focusing on hepatitis C, diagnostic tests, and diagnostic accuracy. Studies were included if they evaluated the sensitivity and specificity of HCV antibody assays in humans, using reference standards such as recombinant immunoblot assays or nucleic acid testing (NAT). Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using the QUADAS tool. 3. Results: A total of 52 studies, encompassing 52,273 unique test measurements, were included. High sensitivity and specificity of HCV antibody RDTs were observed across various screening populations (general population, key populations, hospital patients) and reference standards (EIA, NAT, immunoblot). Limiting the analysis to studies published in the past five or ten years did not alter the results. There was insufficient data to conduct sub-analyses based on HIV co-infection. Oral HCV antibody RDTs demonstrated good sensitivity and specificity compared to blood-based reference standards, making them particularly useful in settings where blood-based testing is challenging. 4. Conclusions: RDTs, including oral tests, exhibit excellent sensitivity and specificity compared to laboratory-based methods for HCV antibody detection across diverse settings. Although the sensitivity of HCV antibody RDTs decreases in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), they remain valuable public health tools for screening purposes. Advances in HCV detection technology present opportunities to enhance screening, referral, and treatment efforts. This review extends previous analyses by including new studies, focusing on oral tests, and evaluating immunoassays using NAT reference standards. 5. Objectives: The primary objective of this review was to identify quantitative evidence on the sensitivity and specificity of RDTs for HCV antibody detection, synthesize the evidence, and inform cost-effectiveness models for different testing strategies. 6. Search Strategy and Study Selection: Observational and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) providing original data from patient specimens were included. The search algorithm targeted hepatitis C, diagnostic tests, and diagnostic accuracy. Databases searched included MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and others. The search was supplemented by contacting researchers and reviewing references of published articles. Study selection involved three stages: screening titles/abstracts, assessing full manuscripts, and independent review by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. 7. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria: Studies were included if they primarily evaluated HCV antibody tests, reported sensitivity and specificity, and were published before May 2015. Excluded studies included those reporting only sensitivity or specificity, conference abstracts, comments, review papers, panel studies, and studies using reference assays only for positive samples. 8. Data Extraction and Analysis: Data extracted included study characteristics (e.g., sample size, setting, sample type, reference standard, manufacturer) and raw cell numbers (true positives, false negatives, false positives, true negatives). Statistical analysis involved calculating sensitivity and specificity for each study and pooling estimates using a bivariate random-effects model. Sub-analyses were conducted based on reference standards, test brands, and combination tests. 9. Study Characteristics: Of the 52 included studies, 41 different brands of testing kits were evaluated. Twelve studies assessed oral fluid RDTs, and 34 studies evaluated point-of-care (POC) tests. The studies spanned various settings and sample types, including venous blood, serum, plasma, and oral fluids. 10. Key Findings: The review identified high diagnostic accuracy of RDTs for HCV antibody detection across diverse populations and settings. Oral RDTs were particularly effective in non-laboratory environments. However, data were insufficient to analyze the impact of HIV co-infection or other co-infections on test performance.
